title: Unpaid Work in the AI Age
gist: Diane Coyle argues the AI-disruption debate has a blind spot: it ignores unpaid 'household production' — including time lost to government bureaucracy and private-sector administration — which is barely measured, and where AI-driven productivity gains could expand leisure with real macroeconomic consequences.

insights.claim: Discussions of how AI will disrupt the economy largely fail to account for valuable activities people perform outside of paid work, making current AI impact estimates structurally incomplete.
insights.speaker: Diane Coyle
insights.so_what: If AI's largest welfare gains land outside measured GDP, headline productivity statistics will understate AI's real economic impact — a reason to distrust GDP-based AI scorecards.
insights.quote: Discussions about how AI might disrupt the economy have a blind spot: they largely fail to account for the valuable activities people do outside of paid work.
insights.locator: CAMBRIDGE—Discussions about how AI might disrupt the economy

insights.claim: Statisticians classify unpaid activities as 'household production' but collect very little data on them, so the category exists in national accounting theory without an empirical base.
insights.speaker: Diane Coyle
insights.so_what: A data gap this large means any AI-and-labor model built only on paid-work series is mis-specified.
insights.quote: Statisticians call such activities “household production,” but they collect very little data about them.

insights.claim: The American Time Use Survey is run annually in the United States but at small scale, and most OECD countries collect such information less frequently, leaving the developed world with thin time-use evidence.
insights.speaker: Diane Coyle
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific data infrastructure that would need to improve before AI's non-market effects can be tracked or traded on.
insights.quote: The American Time Use Survey (ATUS) is conducted annually in the United States, but its scale is small, and most OECD countries collect such information less frequently.

insights.claim: There is very little economic research and next to no policy debate on how most people spend most of their time, meaning the dominant use of human hours is effectively outside the policy conversation.
insights.speaker: Diane Coyle
insights.so_what: An under-researched area is where analytical edge is cheapest — and where policy surprises are most likely when AI shifts time allocation.
insights.quote: there is very little economic research, and next to no policy debate, on how most of us spend most of our time
insights.locator: As a result, there is very little economic research

insights.claim: Unpaid work such as dealing with government bureaucracy and private-sector administration consumes a huge amount of people's free time, and AI tools have the potential to change that with important implications for the economy.
insights.speaker: Diane Coyle
insights.so_what: Points to admin-automation for consumers — benefits, claims, forms, customer service — as an underpriced AI application category with genuine time-value payoff.
insights.quote: Unpaid work, such as dealing with government bureaucracy and private-sector administration, consumes a huge amount of people's free time.
insights.locator: Unpaid work, such as dealing with government bureaucracy
